docs.title: Welcome to NISM-RA Exam Study Center
docs.text:
This study notes has been developed to assist candidates in preparing for the National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) Certification Examination for Research Analyst (NISM-Series-XV: Research Analyst Certification Examination).

Based on Workbook Version: February 2026

Prepared By: Vijoy Vallachira

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Analyst Profession
docs.text:
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:

By the end of this chapter, you should understand:

- Role of a Research Analyst (RA)
- Responsibilities of a Research Analyst
- Principles for interacting with companies and clients
- Essential qualities of a successful Research Analyst

docs.title: 1.1 Primary Role of a Research Analyst
docs.text:
The role of a Research Analyst (RA) is primarily that of a selector. Much like a consumer researching a new phone by comparing brands and technical specifications, an RA collects information from various sources and processes that data to help clients make informed investment decisions.

The core function of an RA involves two distinct stages: Research (the collection of pertinent information) and Analysis (the processing of that data to arrive at a decision).

docs.title: 1.1.1 Data Collection and Sources
docs.text:
Analysts require information at three levels to evaluate an investment:

  • Economic Information: Sourced from government statistics, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and international agencies like the IMF, World Bank, and Asian Development Bank.

  • Industry Information: Sourced from industry-specific journals and professional publications.

  • Company-specific Information: Sourced from financial statements, annual reports, regulatory filings, management Authorizations, plant visits, and stakeholder interviews.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Types of Research Analysts
docs.text:
Analysts are defined by the nature of their analysis, their coverage, and who uses their recommendations.

Type of Analyst Primary Employer Purpose of Research Target Audience Sell-side Analyst Broking firms, Investment Banks Publish reports with specific recommendations (Buy/Hold/Sell) and price targets. Public domain/Clients of the firm. Buy-side Analyst Asset Managers (Mutual Funds, Hedge Funds, Pension Funds) Generate internal investment recommendations for fund managers. Internal consumption only; not available to the public. Independent Analyst Boutique research firms Provide customized research or subscription-based reports. Institutions, regulators, and individual subscribers.

docs.title: 1.2 Primary Responsibilities of a Research Analyst
docs.text: The primary responsibility is to evaluate the growth of economies, industries, and specific companies.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Understanding the Economy
docs.text:
Following Keynesian principles, analysts monitor how government spending and tax rates affect industries. Focus areas include:

  • Macro-economic factors: National income, inflation, interest rates, and unemployment.

  • Policy Impacts: Fiscal and Monetary policies.

  • Capital Flows: Trends in FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) and FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investors).

  • Global Factors: Export/import transactions and their impact on GDP.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Understanding the Industry
docs.text: Analysts must understand the unique growth drivers and challenges of different sectors, including their regulatory environment, business models, competition intensity, and consumer behavior.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Understanding Companies
docs.text:
Companies are evaluated through two primary lenses: Qualitative and Quantitative.

Perspective Focus Areas Examples Qualitative Intangible factors that provide a competitive edge. Management capabilities, brand power, business model strengths, and work ethics. Quantitative Performance metrics captured as numerical data. Revenues, costs, profitability, assets/liabilities, and capacity utilization.

docs.title: 1.3 Basic Principles of Interaction
docs.text:
Direct interaction with company management provides insights into a firm's vision and strategy. However, analysts must cross-verify management claims to avoid being misled by "rosy pictures" designed to influence market prices.

  • Pre-meeting Research: Analysts must be thoroughly familiar with the company's products, industry, competitors, and past annual reports before meeting management.

  • Independence: Opinions must be based on factual information and remain unbiased.

  • Non-public Information: Analysts must explicitly instruct management not to reveal any information that is not available in the public domain.

  • Broad Network: Meaningful inputs should be gathered not just from management, but also from suppliers, distributors, retailers, and customers.

docs.title: 1.3.1 Guidelines for Client Communication
docs.text:
• Realistic View: Suggestions must be based on facts, avoiding overly optimistic or pessimistic bias.

  • Simplicity: Reports should be clear and concise, explaining any jargons or abbreviations.

  • Disclosures: Any conflicts of interest (e.g., if the RA holds shares in the company being researched) must be disclosed beforehand.

docs.title: 1.4 Important Qualities of a Research Analyst
docs.text:
Success in this profession requires a blend of technical skills and specific personality traits.

Core Competencies:

  • Technical: Proficiency in Excel, data analytical tools, and a high degree of comfort with numbers.

  • Conceptual: Clarity in financial concepts and the ability to comprehend complex financial reports.

  • Inquisitive: An enquiring mind capable of asking pertinent questions and paying attention to minute details.

  • Communicative: Strong written and verbal communication skills for presenting recommendations.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Key Distinction: Research is the collection of data; Analysis is the processing of data for decision-making.

  • Economic Barometers: National income, inflation, and interest rates are critical variables for an RA.

  • Agency Risk: RAs help reduce agency risk (the gap between management and ownership) by evaluating "sweat equity" and ESOP impacts.

  • Ethics: SEBI mandates that RAs perform their roles with utmost sincerity, honesty, and ethics.

  • Documentation: It is recommended to use recording devices during management interviews, provided consent is obtained.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
docs.text: This chapter introduces the essential "vocabulary" of finance. While it carries a weightage of 2 marks, these terms are prerequisites for understanding later chapters on financial analysis and valuation.

docs.title: 3.1 Terminology in Equity Market
docs.text: Equity represents ownership and carries higher risks and potentially higher rewards compared to debt.

docs.title: I. Values and Prices
docs.text:
Face Value (FV): The nominal price of a share. It is used to calculate dividends (e.g., a 30% dividend on a ₹10 FV share is ₹3).

Book Value (BV): The "accounting value" or net-worth per share. It is the theoretical amount each share would get if the company wound up today.

Market Value: The current price at which a share trades in the stock market.

Intrinsic Value: The estimated "true" value of a share based on future earning potential. Investors buy when Intrinsic Value > Market Value (undervalued).

Replacement Value: The cost to set up an identical company with similar infrastructure today.

docs.title: II. Valuation Metrics and Ratios
docs.text:
These metrics help analysts determine if a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its peers or history.

Metric Formula Significance Market Cap \(\text{CMP} \times \text{Outstanding Shares}\) The total value the market places on the company. Enterprise Value (EV) \((\text{MV of Equity} + \text{Debt} + \text{Pref. Cap}) - \text{Cash}\) The theoretical cost to buy the entire business. EPS \(\text{Net Profit} / \text{Outstanding Shares}\) The amount of profit earned for every share issued. P/E Ratio \(\text{CMP} / \text{EPS}\) Measures what the market pays for ₹1 of earnings. P/S Ratio \(\text{CMP} / \text{Annual Net Sales per Share}\) Useful for valuing companies with temporary losses. P/BV Ratio \(\text{CMP} / \text{Book Value per Share}\) Common in banking/finance where assets are monetary.

docs.title: 3.2 Terminology in Debt Market
docs.text: Debt represents a loan to an issuer. The primary risks are Interest Rate Risk (price volatility) and Credit Risk (default risk).

docs.title: I. Key Definitions
docs.text:
Coupon Rate: The fixed interest rate paid as a percentage of the Face Value.

Yield to Maturity (YTM): The total return expected if the bond is held until maturity, equating future cash flows to the current market price.

Duration: A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes.

Rule: If interest rates rise, bond prices fall; bonds with higher duration fall more.

docs.title: II. Yield Comparisons
docs.text: Type of Yield Calculation Basis Shortcoming Current Yield \(\text{Coupon} / \text{Market Price}\) Ignores future cash flows and time value. YTM Internal Rate of Return (IRR) Assumes all coupons are reinvested at the same rate. Realised Yield Actual holding period return Requires knowing the actual reinvestment rate.

docs.title: 3.3 Types of Bonds and Their Features
docs.text:
Companies and governments modify bond features to attract different types of investors.

Bond Type Key Characteristic Zero-Coupon Issued at a discount and redeemed at par; pays no periodic interest. Floating-Rate Coupon is reset periodically based on a benchmark (e.g., inflation). Convertible Can be converted into equity shares at a later date, potentially diluting EPS. Inflation-Protected Both principal and interest are adjusted for inflation (e.g., WPI or CPI). Masala Bonds Rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities in foreign markets. Perpetual (AT1) No fixed maturity; coupons are paid only from distributable profits.

docs.title: 3.4 Terminology in Commodity Markets
docs.text:
Spot Price: The current market price for immediate delivery.

Basis: The difference between the spot price and the futures price.

\(\text{Basis} = \text{Spot} - \text{Futures}\)).

Contango: A situation where futures prices are higher than spot prices.

Backwardation: A situation where futures prices are lower than spot prices.

Cost of Carry: The cost of storing, insuring, and financing a physical commodity until delivery.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
Inverse Relationship: Market interest rates and bond prices move in opposite directions.

Agency Risk Reduction: ESOPs and Sweat Equity align management interests with shareholders.

DVRs: Shares with Differential Voting Rights usually trade at a discount to common shares.

TTM: "Trailing Twelve Months" refers to the immediate previous 12 months used for current earnings analysis.

Capital Protection: PPNs (Principal-Protected Notes) aim to protect the initial investment but are still subject to the credit risk of the issuer.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Fundamentals of Research
docs.text: Research acts as the essential link between vast amounts of market data and the formulation of informed investment strategies. This chapter explores the methodologies and philosophies used to evaluate financial assets and commodities.

docs.title: 4.1 Defining Investment Activity
docs.text: Investment in the securities market involves the upfront commitment of a sum of money to earn returns over a specific horizon. This process requires a rigorous analysis of the underlying security's safety, risk, income potential, and growth prospects.

docs.title: I. Investing vs. Trading vs. Speculating
docs.text:
The workbook distinguishes between these three activities based on the participant's motivation, time horizon, and reliance on fundamental value.

Feature Investing Trading Speculating Primary Goal Long-term growth in asset value and cash flows. Profiting from price spreads and historical patterns. Profiting from short-term movements based on a "hunch". Time Horizon Long-term. Short-term (hours to weeks). Very short-term. Key Driver Fundamental value and risk reduction. Price anomalies and statistical patterns. Calculated guesses and incomplete information.

docs.title: II. Active vs. Passive Investing
docs.text:
Active Investing: This strategy involves identifying specific securities priced below their

intrinsic value to outperform the broader asset class. It requires constant evaluation and typically involves a higher volume of transactions.

Passive Investing: This approach aims to match the performance of a specific asset class, often by tracking a market index like the Nifty 50. Analysis is limited to the asset class level rather than individual stocks.

docs.title: 4.2 The Role of Research and Ethical Boundaries
docs.text: The fundamental research process is divided into two parts: Research (obtaining information via reports, site visits, or interviews) and Analysis (processing that data to reach a conclusion).

docs.title: Insider Information vs. Mosaic Analysis
docs.text:
Analysts must navigate the ethical boundary between gaining a competitive edge and using illegal information.

Insider Information: This is material, non-public information that would immediately affect an investor's decision if it were made public. Trading on such information is illegal.

Mosaic Analysis: This is the legal practice of collecting multiple pieces of public information and non-material, non-public information to form a critical insight. The "mosaic" is the final picture created by piecing together these smaller, individually insignificant bits of data.

docs.title: 4.3 Technical Analysis
docs.text:
Technical analysis assumes that all relevant information is already reflected in the stock price. Its primary focus is forecasting price direction through the study of historical market data, specifically price and volume.

Three Essential Elements of Technical Analysis:

  1. Price History: Provides indications of the underlying trend and its direction.

  2. Volume: Indicates the strength of a price movement; trends not supported by volume are often considered weak.

  3. Time Span: The period over which price and volume reflect the impact of market factors.

Key Tools:

  • Price Charts: Line, bar, and candlestick charts are used to visualize patterns.

  • Support and Resistance: Psychological levels where buying or selling interest is concentrated.

  • Trends: Identifying whether the market is moving upwards, downwards, or sideways.

docs.title: 4.4 Fundamental Analysis
docs.text: Unlike technical analysis, fundamental analysis focuses on the long-term potential of an asset to generate profits and cash flows. It operates on the premise that a company's value is driven by its ability to generate future earnings.

docs.title: I. The E-I-C Framework
docs.text:
Comprehensive fundamental research is organized into three analytical baskets:

  1. Economic Analysis: Studying macro-economic trends (GDP, inflation, interest rates) to see if the environment is conducive to growth.

  2. Industry Analysis: Evaluating competition intensity and whether current players can thrive.

  3. Company Analysis: Assessing a firm's financial position, management capabilities, and governance structure.

docs.title: 4.5 Quantitative and Behavioural Approaches
docs.text:
• Quantitative Research: Uses mathematical and statistical models (econometrics) to analyze financial and operational metrics. A major limitation is that frequent changes in accounting standards make historical data difficult to compare with the present.

  • Behavioural Approach: This philosophy suggests that security prices deviate from their fair value because of the fear and greed of participants. Decisions are often influenced by psychological biases rather than pure logic.

docs.title: 4.6 Fundamental Analysis of Commodities
docs.text:
Commodity research focuses on the economic, political, and natural factors influencing supply and demand.

Driver Type Focus Areas Supply Factors Farm production, mine output, weather (floods/droughts), government tariffs, and geopolitical events (sanctions/wars). Demand Factors Global GDP growth, population growth, urbanization, and seasonal needs (e.g., fuel in winter). Macro Indicators Inflation (commodities act as a hedge), Interest Rates (higher rates strengthen the USD, typically lowering commodity prices), and industrial production data.

docs.title: 4.7 Case Studies and Historical Market Impact
I. Gold and Crude Oil
docs.text:
• Gold: Viewed as an inflation hedge and a "safe-haven" asset. It typically has an inverse relationship with stocks, bonds, and currencies. Major demand sectors include Jewelry (47%), Investment (24%), and Central Bank Reserves (23%).

  • Crude Oil: Often called "Black Gold," its quality is determined by density (API gravity) and sulphur content. WTI is a high-quality US-traded oil, while Brent is the benchmark for Europe and Africa.

docs.title: II. Negative Oil Prices (April 20, 2020)
docs.text: WTI crude oil prices briefly turned negative because a global COVID-19 lockdown eliminated demand. Since the WTI contract was deliverable at Cushing, Oklahoma, and storage capacity reached its limit, buyers were not ready to take physical delivery, resulting in a selling spree that pushed prices below zero.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Investing Principle: Profits come from identifying a good investment and making that investment at the right price.

  • Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH): Fundamental analysis contradicts EMH, which claims prices already reflect all relevant info.

  • Technical Philosophy: "Price moves in trends" and "History repeats itself".

  • Mosaic Analysis Rule: It is legal to piece together small bits of non-material info to gain a "big picture" insight.

  • Commodity Indicator: A fall in copper prices often signals a global slowdown in industrial demand.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Economic Analysis
docs.text: Economics is the study of how individuals and societies make choices under conditions of scarcity. It begins with the assumption that people are rational actors with well-defined goals who must face trade-offs because resources—both human and material—are limited. Economic analysis is typically divided into two branches: Microeconomics (focused on individual units) and Macroeconomics (focused on the aggregate economy).

docs.title: 5.1 Basic Principles of Microeconomics
docs.text:
Microeconomics studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources.

  • Consumer Demand: It posits that prices and production levels are driven by what individuals choose to buy and consume.

  • Theory of the Firm: It examines how individual businesses adopt strategies related to inputs, outputs, and production levels to maximize profits.

  • Price Determination: It explains how the interaction between producers and consumers determines the prices of specific goods and services.

docs.title: 5.2 Basic Principles of Macroeconomics
docs.text:
Macroeconomics focuses on "the big picture" by examining factors that influence the aggregate supply and demand of an entire nation.

  • Key Focus Areas: Analysts track aggregate variables such as the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), unemployment rates, national savings, and overall inflation levels.

  • Policy Influence: Macroeconomic performance is heavily influenced by Fiscal Policy (government spending and taxes) and Monetary Policy (central bank actions regarding money supply and interest rates).

docs.title: 5.3 Introduction to Various Macroeconomic Variables
docs.text: Policy makers strive for economic stability through low unemployment, price stability (low inflation), and steady growth.

docs.title: I. National Income (GDP and GNP)
docs.text:
National income is the primary measure of an economy's performance.

  • Gross Domestic Product (GDP): The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders, regardless of the nationality of the producer.

  • Gross National Product (GNP): The market value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, regardless of where they are located in the world.

  • Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA): The difference between GDP and GNP (\(GNP = GDP + NFIA\)).

Methods of Measuring GDP

Method Approach Calculation Basis Product Method Sector-wise Output Sum of the money value of all "final goods" produced in sectors like agriculture, industry, and services. Income Method Aggregate Income Sum of all wages/salaries (employees), professional fees, profits (entrepreneurs), and rent/interest (investors). Expenditure Method Consumption Sum of private consumption, government spending, gross capital formation, and net exports.

docs.title: II. Savings and Investments
docs.text:
Savings represent the portion of income not spent on current consumption.

  • Constituents: National saving is the sum of personal savings (individuals), corporate savings (undistributed profits), and public savings (government).

  • Conversion: Savings are channelled into Investments through financial instruments like equity and bonds to fund productive activities.

docs.title: III. Inflation and Interest Rates
docs.text:
Inflation is the general increase in price levels leading to the erosion of the purchasing power of money.

  • Demand-Pull Inflation: Caused by demand exceeding available supply.

  • Cost-Push Inflation: Caused by an increase in the cost of inputs (raw materials, labor).

  • Measurement: Tracked via the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

  • Relationship with Rates: Higher inflation often forces central banks to raise interest rates to encourage saving and cool down consumption.

docs.title: IV. Capital Flows: FDI and FPI
docs.text: Feature Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) Nature Active and stable; long-term commitment. Passive and volatile; "hot money". Control Investing entities participate in management decisions. Investment in markets (equity/bonds) without management involvement. Benefits Job creation, new technology, and managerial skills. Provides liquidity to the local capital markets.

docs.title: V. Fiscal Policy
docs.text:
Fiscal policy involves government decisions regarding revenue (taxation) and expenditure (infrastructure, welfare).

  • Fiscal Deficit: Occurs when the government's expenditure exceeds its recurring revenue; it is bridged through market borrowings.

  • Current Account Deficit (CAD): The difference between recurring revenue receipts from abroad and payments made to entities abroad. A high CAD can weaken a nation's currency.

Types of Fiscal Policy Stances

Policy Stance Condition Action Expansionary Recession / Slow growth Lower taxes and higher spending to put money in the hands of citizens. Contractionary High Inflation / Overheating Higher taxes and lower spending to cool the economy. Neutral Equilibrium Income and expenditure are balanced; no major changes needed.

docs.title: VI. Monetary Policy
docs.text:
Administered by the central bank (RBI in India), it manages money supply and interest rates.

Common Monetary Policy Tools

Tool Description Repo Rate The rate at which the RBI lends money to banks against securities. Reverse Repo The rate at which the RBI borrows money from banks against securities. Bank Rate The rate for long-term lending to banks without collateral. CRR & SLR Cash Reserve Ratio (cash held with RBI) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (liquid assets like gold/G-Secs held by banks).

docs.title: 5.4 Role of Economic Analysis in Fundamental Analysis
docs.text:
Economic analysis provides the context for evaluating a business's growth potential.

  • External Environment: GDP growth rates indicate the health of the broader market, while inflation and interest rates reveal the cost of capital and consumption strength.

  • Policy Room: High inflation or a large fiscal deficit can signal that the government or central bank has little room to stimulate the economy further.

docs.title: 5.5 Secular, Cyclical, and Seasonal Trends
docs.text:
Economic movements are categorized by their duration and predictability.

  • Secular Trends: Long-term shifts (7–10 years) often caused by technological disruptions, demographic changes, or cultural shifts (e.g., digitalization).

  • Seasonal Trends: Highly predictable annual patterns linked to weather or agriculture (e.g., higher GDP contribution from agriculture during harvest seasons).

  • Cyclical Trends: Medium-term fluctuations (2–6 years) that reverse over time.

The Four Phases of the Economic Cycle

  1. Expansion (Boom): Characterized by high consumer confidence, increased production, and rising inflation/interest rates.

  2. Slow Down: Higher prices and interest rates begin to discourage consumption; capacity utilization rates start to fall.

  3. Recession: Declining consumption leads to layoffs and falling interest rates/inflation; businesses halt expansion.

  4. Recovery: Low inflation allows for loose monetary policy; economic activity picks up as consumers begin buying again.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Standard of Living: Per Capita Income (National Income / Total Population) is a better measure of standard of living than total GDP.

  • Service Sector: Constitutes approximately 60% of India's GDP at factor cost.

  • BOP Structure: The Balance of Payments now follows the IMF (BPM6) structure, dividing transactions into Current, Capital, and Financial accounts.

  • Globalization: The ability to produce and sell anything anywhere; it promotes resource efficiency but increases the risk of "contagion" from global crises.

  • Inventory Cycle: Short-term fluctuations within a commodity cycle caused by producers or customers adjusting their stock levels.

  • Key Information Sources: Major sources include government websites (RBI, SEBI, MOF), the Economic Survey, and published research reports.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Industry Analysis
docs.text: Industry analysis acts as the critical bridge between macro-economic analysis and individual company research. While economic analysis determines if the overall environment is growing, industry analysis identifies which specific sectors will thrive or struggle within that environment.

docs.title: 6.1 Role of Industry Analysis in Fundamental Research
docs.text:
Industry analysis evaluates the specific external factors that influence a group of similar businesses. Analysts must address several key questions:

  • Industry Definition: What exactly is the industry scope?

  • Cyclicality: How sensitive is the sector to economic booms and busts?

  • Market Sizing: What is the potential for growth versus current penetration?

  • Competitive Landscape: What is the level of rivalry and pricing power?

  • Value Migration: Are secular trends shifting profit from one sector to another?

docs.title: 6.2 Defining the Industry and Sectors
docs.text:
Defining an industry is challenging because standard classification systems like the National Industry Classification (NIC) or Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) may not capture the competitive substance of a business.

Term Scope Example Economic Sector Broad segments of the national income. Agriculture, Manufacturing, Services. Business Sector A broad category of related industries. Financial Services (includes Banking, Insurance, etc.). Industry Firms offering similar products to serve the same need. Auto Industry, Steel Industry.

The Definition Challenge:

Analysts must look beyond product types to customer needs. For example, PVR Limited can be defined narrowly as a "Cinema Exhibitor" or broadly as "Out of Home (OOH) Entertainment," which includes live theater and sporting leagues. Similarly, the camera industry was disrupted because it failed to recognize competition from mobile phones.

docs.title: 6.3 Understanding Industry Cyclicality
docs.text:
Industries are categorized by their "income elasticity," or how much demand changes when consumer income rises or falls.

  1. Defensive Industries: Products with low income elasticity. Demand remains stable regardless of the economy (e.g., Healthcare, Food, Agricultural inputs).

  2. Semi-Cyclical Industries: Experience growth during booms and decline during recessions but maintain a "base level" of demand (e.g., Consumer Durables).

  3. Deep Cyclical Industries: Highly sensitive to economic and commodity cycles. They suffer during recessions but see massive growth during recovery due to pent-up demand (e.g., Capital Goods, Steel).

docs.title: 6.4 Market Sizing and Trend Analysis
docs.text:
Analysts use two primary approaches to measure an industry's potential:

  • Top-Down Approach: Starts with macro-factors (e.g., total population) and narrows down to potential users and average expenditure.

  • Bottom-Up Approach: Aggregates the reported data of all individual companies in the sector to arrive at total industry revenue.

docs.title: 6.5 Secular Trends and Value Migration
docs.text:
Secular trends are long-term shifts (occurring once every 7–10 years) that permanently change how goods are produced or consumed.

Drivers of Secular Trends:

  • Technology: e.g., Digital cameras making film obsolete; Shale gas drilling lowering energy costs.

  • Demographics: e.g., An aging population in Japan reducing beer consumption.

  • Culture: e.g., Shift toward western clothing in Asia or organic foods.

Value Migration:

This happens when a phenomenon creates a long-term advantage for one entity at the cost of others.

  • Geographic: Value shifting to low-cost hubs like China.

  • Cross-Industry: e.g., Digital photography destroying the film roll industry (Kodak).

  • Across Value Chain: e.g., High competition in Indian telecom reducing carrier profits but benefiting digital content providers.

docs.title: I. Michael Porter’s Five Force Model
docs.text:
This model determines an industry's attractiveness and long-term profitability.

Force Impact on Profitability Industry Rivalry High rivalry (many players, standard products) leads to lower pricing power. Threat of Substitutes High if switching costs are low (e.g., SMS replacing Telegrams). Bargaining Power of Buyers High if there are many sellers and few buyers (e.g., Government as a buyer). Bargaining Power of Suppliers High if the input is critical or controlled by a few (e.g., OPEC for Crude Oil). Barriers to Entry (Moat) High barriers (licensing, high capital, strong brands) protect profits.

docs.title: II. PESTLE Analysis
docs.text:
Evaluates the external macro-environmental factors.

  • Political: Stability, corruption levels, and fiscal policy.

  • Economic: GDP contributors, inflation, interest rates, and trade balance.

  • Socio-Cultural: Demographics, lifestyle factors, and education.

  • Technological: R&D activity and digital infrastructure.

  • Legal: Transparency in legal architecture and enforcement of laws.

  • Environmental: Pollution control, waste disposal, and ESG compliance.

docs.title: III. BCG Matrix
docs.text:
Classifies business segments based on Market Growth and Market Share.

  • Stars: High growth, high share. Require investment but generate high cash.

  • Cash Cows: Low growth, high share. Stable, steady cash generators (e.g., Colgate, Navneet Publications).

  • Question Marks: High growth, low share. Risky; require strategy to become Stars.

  • Dogs: Low growth, low share. Low cash generation.

docs.title: 6.7 Key Industry Drivers and KPIs
docs.text: Industry Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Airlines/Logistics Passenger/Cargo km, Occupancy rate, Price per km. Banking/NBFC NIM (Net Interest Margin), NPA Ratio, CASA Ratio, Capital Adequacy. IT Services FTE (Full Time Equivalent) billing, Attrition rate, Revenue per FTE. Retail Number of stores, Same-Store Sales Growth (SSSG). Telecom ARPU (Average Revenue Per User), Subscriber Churn rate.

docs.title: Direct Taxes
docs.text:
• Corporate Income Tax: Standard rate is 30% (or 25% for turnover below ₹400 cr).

  • MAT (Minimum Alternate Tax): Payable if income tax is less than 15% of book profits.

  • Surcharge: 12% if income is above ₹10 cr; 7% if between ₹1 cr and ₹10 cr.

  • Cess: 4% Health and Education cess.

docs.title: Indirect Taxes
docs.text:
• GST: Most goods are taxed at 18%.

  • Excise & VAT: Still applicable to liquor, petrol, and diesel.

  • STT (Securities Transaction Tax): Paid at the time of selling securities.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• The "Moat": A term popularized by Warren Buffett referring to high barriers to entry that protect a business from competitors.

  • Role Reversal: In SCP analysis, Structure determines Conduct, which in turn results in Performance (RoE, RoIC).

  • Road Tax: A lifetime tax paid upfront by automobile purchasers that can impact downstream auto-ancillary demand.

  • Going Concern: If a company is loss-making and a turnaround is unlikely, it is valued at liquidation value rather than EV/Sales.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Company Analysis – Business and Governance
docs.text: Company analysis is the final, granular level of the E-I-C (Economy-Industry-Company) framework. While macro and industry factors set the stage, company-specific factors determine which individual business will outperform its peers.

docs.title: 7.1 Role of Company Analysis in Fundamental Research
docs.text: Analysts focus on internal drivers such as business models, management quality, and competitive advantages to assess if a company can exploit industry opportunities and withstand external threats. This qualitative study provides the context needed before diving into the numerical financial analysis.

docs.title: 7.2 Understanding Business and Business Models
docs.text: Analysts must start with a fundamental question: "Do I understand the business?". - Core Logic: Research should prioritize firms whose products, customers, and delivery mechanisms are clear. - Sector Specificity: Each industry has unique KPIs. For example, Footfalls are critical for Retail, Net Interest Margin (NIM) for Banking, and Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) for Telecom. - Model vs. Product: Competition is often between business models (how value is created/delivered) rather than just the products themselves.

docs.title: 7.3 Pricing Power and Sustainability
docs.text: Pricing Power is the ability to independently determine prices without losing customers to competitors. - Drivers: It is influenced by industry factors (competition intensity) and company-specific factors like brand loyalty and a low-cost base. - Impact: Companies with high pricing power can pass on raw material cost escalations to customers, protecting their profit margins.

docs.title: 7.4 Competitive Advantages and Differentiation
docs.text:
To outperform, a company must distinguish itself in three primary areas:

Area of Differentiation Focus Key Driver Product Differentiation Unique features, quality, or functionality. Strong R&D and a culture of innovation. Competitive Pricing Offering better value for money than peers. Operational efficiency and a low-cost advantage. Execution Better branding, sales strategy, and positioning. Management track record and sales force focus.

docs.title: 7.5 SWOT Analysis Framework
docs.text:
SWOT analysis evaluates internal capabilities versus external dynamics.

  • Strengths (Internal): Financial strength, patents (IP), low customer concentration, and strong track record.
  • Weaknesses (Internal): High fixed costs, weak margins, high debt, or lack of experience in new segments.
  • Opportunities (External): Technological shifts, geographical expansion, or industry consolidation.
  • Threats (External): Economic recession, regulatory changes, or disruptive new technologies.

docs.title: 7.6 Quality of Management and Governance
docs.text: Because ownership is separate from management, Agency Risk exists—the risk that managers may not act in the best interest of owners.

docs.title: I. Evaluating Management Competency
docs.text: Analysts assess "C-level" executives based on: - Experience & Track Record: Past performance in similar roles. - Vision: Long-term strategic direction and goal-setting. - Execution: History of meeting or exceeding stated guidance. - Succession Planning: Plans for continuity if top management leaves.

docs.title: II. Corporate Governance Standards
docs.text: These are the rules and processes that ensure a company is run ethically. Key indicators include: - Board Composition: At least 1/3 to 1/2 of the board should be Independent Directors. - Role Separation: The Chairman of the Board should ideally not be the CEO/MD (mandated for the top 1,000 listed companies). - Auditor Integrity: Auditors should be rotated every 5 years and not be overly dependent on the fees from a single group. - Related Party Transactions: Transactions with promoter-owned entities must be at "arms-length" and reviewed by the audit committee.

docs.title: 7.7 Business Risks
docs.text: Analysts must constantly ask: "What could go wrong?". A good management team is transparent about risks—such as currency fluctuations or execution delays—and has mitigation strategies in place.

docs.title: 7.8 Credit Rating History
docs.text: A company's Credit Rating indicates its ability to service debt. Tracking changes in these ratings over time reveals financial risk levels and how responsive management is to the concerns raised by rating agencies.

docs.title: 7.9 ESG Framework (Environment, Social, and Governance)
docs.text: Modern investors use ESG filters to identify sustainable businesses. - Environmental: Carbon footprint, pollution control, and resource efficiency. - Social: Human rights, gender equality, and community relations. - Governance: Ethics and shareholder rights. - Regulatory Note: SEBI now mandates top 1,000 companies to provide ESG disclosures via the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Moat: A term for high entry barriers that protect a company's "economic castle".
  • Promoter Pledging: Promoters may take loans against their shares; high pledging can lead to sharp price drops if lenders are forced to sell the collateral.
  • BRSR: The official framework for ESG reporting in India starting FY2023.
  • Arms-Length: A principle requiring transactions between related parties to be conducted as if they were between independent entities.
  • Keyman Risk: The risk to an organization if its leadership is too concentrated in a few individuals without a succession plan.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
docs.text: Financial analysis translates qualitative business assessments into numerical expectations. It involves studying a company’s historical performance to forecast its future ability to generate profits and cash flows.

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction to Financial Statements
docs.text: Financial statements are prepared under accrual accounting, where income is recognized when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands. Under IndAS 1, a complete set includes: - Balance Sheet: Financial position at a specific point in time. - Profit and Loss (P/L) Statement: Financial performance over a period. - Statement of Changes in Equity: Movements in shareholder funds. - Cash Flow Statement: Sources and uses of cash. - Notes to Accounts: Detailed explanations of accounting policies and breakdowns of line items.

docs.title: 8.2 Consolidated vs. Stand-alone Results
docs.text:
• Stand-alone Financials: Represent the financial position of the parent entity alone.
  • Consolidated Financials: Treat a parent company and all its controlled subsidiaries as a single economic unit.
  • Key Insight: Analysts generally prefer consolidated statements as they provide a holistic view of the entire business group's performance.

docs.title: 8.3 The Balance Sheet
docs.text: The balance sheet follows the equation: \(\text{Assets} = \text{Equity} + \text{Liabilities}\).

docs.title: I. Common Asset Classifications
docs.text: Category Definition Key Line Items Non-Current Assets Benefits expected beyond one year. Property, Plant & Equipment (PPE), Goodwill, Intangible Assets, Long-term Investments. Current Assets Benefits expected within one operating cycle (typically one year). Inventory, Trade Receivables, Cash & Cash Equivalents, Short-term Investments.

docs.title: II. Equity and Liabilities
docs.text:
• Equity: Represents residual interest belonging to owners (Share Capital + Reserves).
  • Non-Current Liabilities: Long-term obligations like term loans and bonds due beyond one year.
  • Current Liabilities: Obligations due within one year, such as Trade Payables, short-term debt, and the current portion of long-term debt.

docs.title: III. Balance Sheet Metrics
docs.text:
• Total Debt: Sum of long-term debt, short-term debt, lease obligations, and current maturities.
  • Working Capital: \(\text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}\).
  • Core Working Capital: \(\text{Inventory} + \text{Trade Receivables} - \text{Trade Payables}\). This measures the capital required to sustain core operations.

docs.title: 8.4 The Profit and Loss (P/L) Account
docs.text: The P/L account reveals a company's ability to generate value from its operations.

docs.title: I. Key Profit Metrics
docs.text:
• EBITDA: Earning Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortization. It measures operating efficiency without the impact of capital structure or non-cash charges.
  • EBIT (Operating Profit): EBITDA minus Depreciation and Amortization. Used to measure the ability to service interest.
  • PAT (Net Profit): Final profit available to shareholders after all expenses and taxes.

docs.title: II. Adjusted Profit after Tax
docs.text: Analysts calculate Adjusted PAT by removing the impact of Exceptional Items (one-time, non-recurring events) to understand the company's true sustainable earning power.

docs.title: 8.5 Basics of Cash Flows
docs.text: Cash flows are segregated into three distinct streams: 1. Operating Cash Flows: Cash generated from core business activities (e.g., selling goods). Warning: Continuous negative operating cash flow is an alarming signal of risk. 2. Investing Cash Flows: Cash used for or generated from assets (e.g., buying machinery or selling land). 3. Financing Cash Flows: Cash related to capital structure (e.g., borrowing loans or paying dividends).

docs.title: 8.6 Quality of Accounting: Audit Reports
docs.text: An auditor reviews the financial statements and provides one of three opinions: - Clean Report: No issues found; reflects a "true and fair" view. - Qualified Report: The auditor has specific reservations about certain accounting treatments. - Disclaimer: The auditor is unable to verify parts of the financials due to a lack of information.

docs.title: I. Profitability and Return Ratios
docs.text: Ratio Formula Significance EBITDA Margin \(\text{EBITDA} / \text{Net Sales}\) Measures operating efficiency. Return on Equity (ROE) \(\text{Net Profit} / \text{Average Net-worth}\) Single most important metric for equity investors. Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) \(\text{EBIT} / \text{Average Total Capital}\) Measures overall capital productivity (Equity + Debt).

docs.title: II. Leverage and Liquidity Ratios
docs.text: Ratio Formula Significance Debt/Equity \(\text{Total Debt} / \text{Net-worth}\) Measures financial risk; ideally \(\le 1\). Interest Coverage \(\text{EBIT} / \text{Interest Expense}\) Ability to pay interest from earnings. Current Ratio \(\text{Current Assets} / \text{Current Liabilities}\) Ability to meet short-term obligations. Quick Ratio \((\text{Current Assets} - \text{Inventory}) / \text{Current Liabilities}\) Measures immediate liquidity.

docs.title: 8.8 Dupont Analysis
docs.text: Dupont Analysis decomposes ROE into three drivers to identify how a company is generating returns: $\(\text{ROE} = \text{Net Profit Margin} \times \text{Asset Turnover} \times \text{Financial Leverage}\)$ - Insight: If ROE increases due to higher leverage rather than margin or efficiency, it signals higher risk.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Accrual Basis: Profits in the P/L do not equal cash in the bank.
  • Goodwill: Arises when an acquisition price exceeds the fair value of net assets.
  • Contingent Liabilities: Potential obligations recorded in notes (e.g., lawsuits) but not on the balance sheet.
  • Inventory Turnover: Higher is better; it indicates how fast stock is converted into sales.
  • Insider Activity: If insiders are buying, it is often a strong signal of future profit potential.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary & Market Terminology
docs.text:
For a candidate from a non-financial background, Chapter 3 is arguably the most critical "vocabulary" chapter in the entire workbook. While it only accounts for 2 marks on its own, the terminology introduced here forms the essential language required to understand Chapter 8 (Financial Analysis) and Chapter 10 (Valuation Principles), which together represent 24% of the exam weightage.

Below is an elaboration on the key terms and formulas from the NISM workbook, the primary official public resource for this certification.

docs.title: 1. Equity Market Terminology
docs.text: These terms help you distinguish between what a company is "worth" on paper versus what it costs to "buy" in the market.

docs.title: Intrinsic Value vs. Market Value:
docs.text:
Intrinsic value is the estimated "true" value of a share based on future earning potential, while Market Value is the current trading price in the stock market.

Undervalued:

\(\text{Intrinsic Value} > \text{Market Value}\)

Overvalued:

\(\text{Intrinsic Value} < \text{Market Value}\)

docs.title: Market Capitalization (Market Cap):
docs.text:
This is the total market value of the company’s equity.

Formula:

\(\text{Market Cap} = \text{Current Market Price (CMP)} \times \text{Total Outstanding Shares}\)

docs.title: Enterprise Value (EV):
docs.text:
This represents the theoretical cost to buy the entire business, including its debt, while adjusting for its cash.

Formula (Standalone):

\(\text{EV} = (\text{Market Value of Equity} + \text{Preferred Capital} + \text{Debt}) - (\text{Cash and Cash Equivalents})\)

docs.title: 2. Common Valuation Ratios
docs.text: For a non-financial person, these are the "shorthand" metrics used to quickly judge if a stock is cheap or expensive.

docs.title: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio:
docs.text:
Measures what the market is willing to pay for every ₹1 of profit.

Formula:

\(\text{P/E Ratio} = \frac{\text{Market Price per Share}}{\text{Earnings Per Share (EPS)}}\)

docs.title: Price-to-Book Value (P/BV) Ratio:
docs.text:
Compares the stock price to its "accounting value" (assets minus liabilities).

Formula:

\(\text{P/BV Ratio} = \frac{\text{CMP}}{\text{Book Value per Share}}\)

docs.title: Price-to-Sales (P/S) Ratio:
docs.text:
Useful for valuing companies that aren't profitable yet but have high sales.

Formula:

\(\text{P/S Ratio} = \frac{\text{CMP}}{\text{Annual Net Sales per Share}}\)

docs.title: 3. Debt Market Terminology
docs.text:
Debt involves lending money. The "risk" here is usually about whether you will get your interest and principal back.

Coupon Rate vs. Yield: The Coupon is the fixed interest rate promised on the Face Value (e.g., 8%), whereas the Yield is the actual return based on the price you paid.

Yield to Maturity (YTM): The total interest you expect to earn if you hold the bond until it finishes (matures).

Duration: This measures how sensitive a bond's price is to changes in interest rates.

Rule of Thumb: If interest rates rise, bond prices fall. Higher duration means the price will fall more.

docs.title: 4. Commodity Market Terminology
docs.text:
Contango: When the future price is higher than the current spot price (usually due to storage costs).

Backwardation: When the future price is lower than the current spot price.

Basis: The difference between the current price and the future price.

Formula:

\(\text{Basis} = \text{Spot Price} - \text{Futures Price}\)

docs.title: 2.1 Introduction to Securities and Securities Market
What are Securities?
docs.text:
Securities are tradable financial instruments that represent either:

  • Ownership in an entity (e.g., equity shares), or
  • A debt obligation owed by the issuer to the investor (e.g., bonds, debentures).

They are issued by companies, financial institutions, and governments to raise funds, and are purchased by investors seeking returns on their savings. Securities are also commonly referred to as financial instruments or financial products.

docs.title: Why are Securities Important?
docs.text: Securities serve the interests of both issuers and investors:

docs.title: For Issuers
docs.text:
• Provide access to capital for business expansion, operations, and development.
  • Enable long-term fund raising from a large pool of investors.

docs.title: For Investors
docs.text:
• Convert savings into financial assets capable of generating returns.
  • Offer opportunities for wealth creation and income generation.

Thus, securities create a mutually beneficial relationship between those who need funds and those who have surplus funds to invest.

docs.title: Role of the Secondary Market
docs.text:
One of the major advantages of securities is that investors can transfer their ownership to others through the secondary market without affecting the issuer.

This provides:

  • Liquidity to investors (easy entry and exit)
  • Long-term capital to issuers
  • Flexibility for investors to sell investments whenever needed

As a result, even long-term securities become effectively liquid and tradable investments.

docs.title: What is a Securities Market?
docs.text:
A securities market is an organized platform where buyers and sellers trade securities.

Its primary functions are:

  • Facilitating buying and selling of securities
  • Creating liquidity
  • Enabling efficient movement of capital
  • Converting savings into investments

By bringing together a large number of buyers and sellers, the market helps securities trade at prices close to their fair market value.

docs.title: Economic Importance of Securities Markets
docs.text:
Securities markets play a critical role in the economy by:

  • Mobilizing idle savings
  • Channeling funds into productive activities
  • Supporting business growth and economic development
  • Providing investors with a wide range of investment opportunities

In simple terms, securities markets act as a bridge between savers and borrowers.

docs.title: Components of the Financial Market
docs.text:
The financial market consists of four major participants:

Participant Role Investors / Providers of Funds Supply capital by purchasing securities Borrowers / Seekers of Funds Raise capital by issuing securities Intermediaries Facilitate transactions and settlement Regulatory Bodies Ensure fair, transparent, and orderly market functioning

Examples of intermediaries include stock exchanges, brokers, depositories, and clearing corporations.

docs.title: Definition of Securities under SCRA, 1956
docs.text: Section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (SCRA) defines securities broadly to include:

docs.title: Traditional Securities
docs.text:
• Shares
  • Stocks
  • Bonds
  • Debentures
  • Debenture stock

docs.title: Investment and Market-linked Instruments
docs.text:
• Derivatives
  • Mutual Fund Units
  • Collective Investment Scheme Units
  • Pooled Investment Vehicle Units

docs.title: Specialized Instruments
docs.text:
• Security Receipts
  • Securitized Debt Instruments
  • Government Securities
  • Rights and Interests in Securities
  • Electronic Gold Receipts (declared securities in 2021)

docs.title: Exclusion
docs.text: • Unit Linked Insurance Policies (ULIPs) are specifically excluded from the definition of securities.

docs.title: Broad Categories of Securities
docs.text: Investors in the Indian securities market can choose from three broad categories of securities:

docs.title: 1. Equity Securities
docs.text:
Represent ownership in a company.

Examples:

  • Equity Shares
  • Preference Shares

docs.title: 2. Debt Securities
docs.text:
Represent borrowing by the issuer.

Examples:

  • Bonds
  • Debentures
  • Government Securities

docs.title: 3. Derivative Securities
docs.text:
Derive their value from an underlying asset.

Examples:

  • Futures
  • Options

The choice among these categories depends primarily on an investor's risk appetite, return expectations, and investment objectives.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text: The securities market is a vital mechanism that channels savings into productive investments. It allows issuers to raise funds efficiently while providing investors with opportunities to earn returns, maintain liquidity, and participate in economic growth. Securities can broadly be classified into equity, debt, and derivatives, each catering to different investment needs and risk profiles.

docs.title: SECTIONS
docs.text:
2.2.1 Equity Shares

2.2.2 Debentures/Bonds/Notes

2.2.3 Warrants

2.2.4 Indices

2.2.5 Mutual Fund Units

2.2.6 Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)

2.2.7 Hybrids/Structured Products

2.2.8 Commodities

docs.title: 2.3 Structure of Securities Market
docs.text:
Securities Market = Primary Market + Secondary Market (interdependent and inseparable).

Market Function Primary Market (New Issue Market) Issuers raise capital by issuing securities to investors. Fresh securities issued. Secondary Market Facilitates trades in already-issued securities. Enables exit for investors or entry for new investors.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Primary Market (Detailed)
docs.text: Used by companies (issuers) to raise fresh capital.

docs.title: Types of Offerings:
docs.text: Term Meaning Public issue Securities issued to members of the public; anyone eligible can participate. Retail issue. IPO (Initial Public Offer) First sale of corporate common shares to public. Purpose: raise equity capital for growth. SEBI eligibility criteria apply. FPO (Follow on Public Offer) Already listed company makes fresh issue or offer for sale to public. Private Placement Issuing large quantity of shares to a select set of investors (max 50 as per Companies Act 2013). Rights Issue Securities offered to existing shareholders as on cut-off date. They can buy at specific price. Bonus Issue Additional shares to existing shareholders without any consideration. From retained earnings. Onshore Offering Capital raised from domestic market. Offshore Offering Capital raised from investors outside the country. OFS (Offer for Sale) Existing shareholders (promoters/large investors) offer portion of their holding to public. No fresh issuance. Proceeds go to offerors. Sweat Equity Shares issued to employees, promoters, technocrats as reward (Sec 54, Companies Act 2013). ESOPs Options given to employees to buy shares at pre-determined price after vesting period.

docs.title: IPO Allocation (SEBI):
docs.text:
• At least 35% → retail investors (≤ ₹2,00,000 investment)
  • Up to 50% → Qualified Institutional Investors (QIBs)
  • Balance → other investors

docs.title: Anchor Investor (introduced 2009):
docs.text:
• QIB who applies for ≥ ₹10 crore in a public issue (book building).
  • Can be allocated up to 60% of QIB portion.
  • Bidding opens one day before IPO opens to public.
  • Allocation price can be lower than final issue price.
  • Indicator of offer quality.

docs.title: QIP (Qualified Institutional Placement):
docs.text:
• Private placement of shares by listed company to QIBs only.
  • SEBI defines eligibility, quantum, pricing.

docs.title: Preferential Issue:
docs.text:
• Issue of specified securities to select person/group on private placement basis.
  • Excludes: public issue, rights, bonus, ESOPs, QIP, sweat equity, DRs, foreign securities.
  • Must comply with SEBI pricing, disclosure, lock-in requirements + Companies Act.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Secondary Market (Detailed)
docs.text: Provides liquidity to instruments from primary market. - Dealings are between investors (issuers not involved). - Promotes growth of primary market and capital formation.

docs.title: Two Segments:
docs.text: Segment Meaning OTC Market (Over-the-Counter) Trades directly negotiated between two or more counterparties. Securities traded and settled over the counter. Exchange Traded Market Trading and settlement through stock exchanges. Clearing corporation acts as counterparty and guarantees settlement.

docs.title: Trading:
docs.text:
• Formal contract to buy/sell securities.
  • Indian stock exchanges: electronic order-matching system.

docs.title: Clearing and Settlement:
docs.text:
Term Meaning Clearing Ascertaining net obligations of buyers and sellers for a specific time period. Settlement Delivering shares (by seller) and paying money (by buyer).
  • OTC transactions: settled directly between counterparties.
  • Exchange trades: settled through Clearing Corporation.
  • Full novation: Clearing corporation acts as buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer → substantially reduces counterparty risk.

docs.title: Risk Management (Exchange Traded):
docs.text: Clearing corporation charges various margins: | Margin Type | Meaning | |-------------|---------| | Initial/Upfront Margin | Percentage of transaction value based on Value At Risk (VaR) | | Peak Margin | Additional intraday margin | | Mark-to-Market (MTM) Margin | Notional loss suffered by outstanding trade due to price movements |

docs.title: 2.4 Various Market Participants and Their Activities
2.4.1 Market Intermediaries
docs.text: Intermediary Role Stock Exchanges Provide trading platform (NSE, BSE, MSEI). Electronic anonymous order matching. Appoint clearing agencies and clearing banks. Depositories Hold securities in electronic form (NSDL, CDSL). Provide services related to demat transactions. Depository Participant (DP) Agent of depository. Interfaces with investors. Holds investor-level accounts. Trading Members (Stock Brokers) Registered members of stock exchange. Facilitate buy/sell transactions. Authorised Person (AP) Appointed by stockbroker as agent to reach investors (replaced sub-brokers from April 2019). Custodians Hold funds/securities of large clients (banks, insurance, FPI). Settle transactions, track corporate actions. Clearing Corporation Legal counterparty to all trades. Guarantees settlement. Clearing Banks Maintain accounts for clearing members. Pay-in and pay-out of funds. Merchant Bankers Issue managers, investment bankers, lead managers. Manage new issue process. Underwriters Subscribe to any portion of public offer not bought by investors. Hard vs soft underwriting. Farmer Producer Organizations (FPO) Collective of farmers to improve bargaining power, market access, economic wellbeing.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Institutional Participants
docs.text: Participant Role/Definition FPIs (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Entities outside India registered with SEBI to invest in India. P-Note Participants Instruments issued by SEBI-registered FPIs to overseas investors not registered with SEBI. Mutual Funds Professionally managed collective investment scheme. Pools money to purchase securities. Insurance Companies Life and general insurance. Major investors in equity, G-sec, bonds. Pension Funds Pool of retirement funds. Provide stable long-term growth. Venture Capital Funds Invest in early-stage enterprises with long-term growth potential. Bring managerial/technical expertise. Private Equity Firms Funding for growth, expansion, or buy-outs (includes venture capital). Hedge Funds Wide mandate across assets, products, geographies. Not necessarily hedged. AIFs (Alternative Investment Funds) Category I (start-ups, SMEs, infra), Category II (real estate, PE, no leverage), Category III (hedge funds, use leverage). Investment Advisers Help investors with asset allocation, financial planning, goal setting. Warehouse Service Providers Storage for commodities. Issue negotiable warehouse receipts (NWRs). Registered with WDRA. Quality Assayers Evaluate and certify quality of commodities. Required for NWRs. EPF (Employee Provident Fund) Defined benefit scheme. Mandatory contributions (12% employer + 12% employee). NPS (National Pension Scheme) Government-sponsored retirement scheme. Subscriber chooses funds. Family Offices Handle wealth, investments, estate planning, tax planning for wealthy families. Corporate Treasuries Temporarily invest surplus funds of companies.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Retail Participants
docs.text:
• Individual investors buying/selling for personal account (not for another organization).
  • HNI = High Net-worth Individuals
  • UHNI = Ultra High Net-worth Individuals
  • NRIs, PIOs, QFIs permitted under Automatic Route (RBI).

docs.title: 2.4.4 Corporates
docs.text:
• Processors, manufacturers, importers, exporters.
  • Dependent on commodities.
  • Business margins affected by commodity price variations.
  • Procure raw materials → convert to value-added products.

docs.title: 2.4.5 Proxy Advisory services firms
docs.text:
• Advise investors on exercise of their rights in the company.
  • Recommendations on public offer or voting on agenda items.
  • Analyze voting proposals and how they affect investor interest.
  • Typically engaged by institutional investors.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Cash, Tom and Spot Trades/Transactions
docs.text: Type Settlement Meaning Cash Trades T+0 Same trading day Tom Trades T+1 Next trading day

docs.title: 2.5.2 Forward transactions
docs.text:
• Contractual agreements between two parties.
  • Buy/sell underlying asset at a future date at a price decided today.
  • Both parties obliged to honour.
  • OTC contracts (customized terms).
  • Carry counterparty risk.

Example: Farmer agrees to sell wheat to miller 6 months later at a price agreed today.

docs.title: 2.5.3 Futures
docs.text:
• Standardized exchange-traded forward contracts.
  • Standardized: market lots, quality, delivery terms, settlement method.
  • Traded and settled on stock exchange.
  • Clearing corporation provides settlement guarantee.
  • Subject to stringent margin requirements.
  • Available on: equities, equity indices, commodities, currencies, interest rates.

Example (MCX Wheat Futures): - Trading unit: 10MT - Delivery: physical only - Delivery centre: Exchange approved warehouses

docs.title: 2.5.4 Options
docs.text:
Definition: - Contract that gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell underlying asset on or before a stated date at a stated price.

Parties: | Party | Action | |-------|--------| | Buyer/Holder | Pays premium, buys the right | | Writer/Seller | Receives premium, has obligation to sell/buy if buyer exercises |

Types: | Type | Right | |------|-------| | Call Option | Right to BUY underlying at strike price on or before given date | | Put Option | Right to SELL underlying at strike price on or before given date |

Can be transacted: OTC Market OR Exchange Traded Markets.

Example: Arvind buys Nifty 50 call option at 11000, 3 months, pays ₹100 premium. - If Nifty at 11200 on settlement: In the money → exercise → gain = (200 - 100) = ₹100 net. - If Nifty at 10800: Out of money → expires worthless → Arvind loses ₹100 premium.

docs.title: 2.5.5 Swaps
docs.text:
Definition: - Derivative contract between two parties to exchange cash flows in the future according to pre-arranged formula. - Helps manage risks: interest rates, currency rates, commodity prices.

Example (Interest Rate Swap): - Borrower pays floating rate (T-bill rate + spread) on borrowing. - Borrower prefers fixed rate. - Enters swap: Pay fixed to swap dealer, receive T-bill + spread from swap dealer. - Net obligation = fixed rate to swap dealer.

docs.title: 2.5.6 Trading, Speculating, Hedging, Arbitrage, Pledging of Shares
docs.text: Term Definition Trading Short-term (hours/days/weeks). Based on price patterns from technical analysis. Assumes historical patterns repeat. Higher probability of gains than speculators. Speculating Purchase/sale expecting gain from price changes. Based on private/insider information or own view on fundamentals. Usually short-term. Leveraged (magnifies gains/losses). Hedging Buying asset/contract to offset potential losses from existing investment. Expected result: no gain/no loss. Goal: avoid losses, not make profits. Uses forwards/futures, swaps, options. Arbitrage Simultaneous purchase and sale in two different markets to profit from price discrepancies. Exists only briefly in efficient markets. Pledging of Shares Taking loan against securities. Pledgor = investor. Pledgee = lender. Securities remain in demat account but blocked. Can be unpledged when loan repaid. Default → pledgee can sell shares after notice.

docs.title: 2.6 Dematerialization and Rematerialization of securities
docs.text: Term Meaning Dematerialization Converting physical securities into book entry (electronic) form. No distinctive numbers, folio numbers, certificate numbers. SEBI requires public issue companies to offer demat option. Rematerialization Converting electronic securities back into physical form. Securities allotted with distinctive numbers.

docs.title: 2.2.2.1 Foreign bonds (Detailed)
docs.text:
Aspect Details Issuers Companies, Government, SPVs Investors Institutional and Individual Medium Direct issuance through Stock Exchanges Regulator Regulators in respective country of issue

Key Features:

  • Issued by a company in a currency different from its home currency.
  • Denominated in the currency of the country where it is issued.
  • Example: Delhi International Airport Limited (GMR SPV) issued USD bonds in US.

Risk for Issuer:

  • Creates significant foreign currency risk.
  • If foreign currency appreciates against domestic currency, issuer needs more domestic currency to repay.

Why companies do it:

  • USD or other mature economy currencies carry significantly lower interest rates than emerging markets.

docs.title: 2.2.2.2 Euro bonds / External Bonds (Detailed)
docs.text:
Aspect Details Issuers Companies, Government, SPVs Investors Institutional and Individual Medium Direct issuance through Stock Exchanges Regulator Regulators in respective country of issue

Key Features:

  • Issued in a currency different from the currency of the country in which it is issued.
  • Example: US dollar denominated bonds issued in Kuwait (currency = Kuwaiti Dinar).

Masala Bonds (Special Category):

  • Euro bonds denominated in Indian Rupees (INR)
  • Issued outside India
  • First issued: November 2014 by International Finance Corporation
  • Listed on London Stock Exchange

Key Difference from Foreign Bonds:

Foreign Bonds Masala Bonds (Euro Bonds) Currency risk bearer Issuer Investor Reason If foreign currency appreciates If INR depreciates against investor's local currency

docs.title: 2.2.3 Warrants
docs.text:
Aspect Details Issuer Companies Investors Institutional and Individual Medium Direct issuance through Stock Exchanges Regulator SEBI

Definition:

  • Provides the right, but not the obligation, to buy equity shares of the issuer company.
  • After a specified period of time.
  • At a pre-determined price.

docs.title: 2.2.4 Indices
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Tracks market movement using prices of a specific number of shares chosen as representative sample.
  • Most leading indices are weighted by market capitalisation.

Most widely tracked indices in India:

Index Exchange Number of Stocks Nifty 50 NSE 50 S&P BSE Sensex BSE 30 SX40 MSEI 40

Other common indices:

  • Nifty Next 50, Nifty 100, Nifty 500
  • S&P BSE 100, BSE 500, BSE MidCap, BSE SmallCap
  • Sector indices (Banking, IT, Pharma, FMCG, etc.)

Major Uses of Indices:

  1. Reference point to compare returns of other asset classes (gold, debt)
  2. Benchmark to compare returns of active equity fund/portfolio
  3. Barometer of the economy or a sector
  4. Real-time indicator of market sentiments
  5. Underlying for Index Funds, Index Futures and Options

docs.title: 2.2.5 Mutual Fund Units
docs.text:
Aspect Details Issuer Mutual Funds Investors Institutional and Individual Medium Direct issuance by mutual funds Regulator SEBI

Definition:

  • Investment vehicle that pools money from many investors.
  • Invests the pool in a portfolio of assets reflecting a common theme/objective.
  • Each investor's share = unit.

Net Asset Value (NAV):

  • Value of each unit.
  • Changes continuously reflecting changes in portfolio value.

Types:

Type Meaning Open-ended Buy from fund anytime; sell back to fund anytime; no fixed maturity Close-ended Fixed maturity period; limited liquidity

docs.title: 2.2.6 Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)
docs.text:
Aspect Details Issuer Mutual Funds Investors Institutional and Individual Medium Direct issuance + marketed by Authorised Participants Regulator SEBI

Definition:

  • Investment vehicle that invests pooled money to track an index, commodity (e.g., Gold), or basket of assets.

Key Features:

  • Like an index fund (portfolio reflects index it tracks)
  • Unlike index fund: Units are listed and traded on stock exchange
  • Price changes continuously (like regular shares)

Creation Process:

  1. Sponsor (MF or global asset manager)
  2. Authorised Participants (large broking houses, international banks) create bundle of assets
  3. Authorised Participants deliver bundle to sponsor
  4. Sponsor issues ETF units
  5. ETF units sold to retail investors and traded like regular shares

Advantages:

  • Diversification benefits of index fund
  • Can buy/sell even one unit at real-time prices
  • Passively managed → lower expense ratios than mutual funds

docs.title: 2.2.7.1 Preference Shares
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Special kind of equity shares with preference over common/ordinary equity shares at:
    • Time of dividend
    • Time of repayment of capital in winding up

Dual Nature:

Like Equity Like Debt Called shareholders (not creditors) Pre-determined rate of dividend Payment called "dividend" Dividend payable before common equity Paid from Profit After Tax (PAT) Preference in winding up (after debt, before equity) Not an obligation unlike interest

What they DO NOT have:

  • Voting rights
  • Right over residual assets in winding up

Types:

  • Cumulative (unpaid dividend carried forward)
  • Non-cumulative (unpaid dividend lapses)
  • Convertible (partly or fully)

docs.title: 2.2.7.2 Convertible Debentures & Bonds
docs.text:
Definition: - Debt instruments that can be converted into equity shares at a future date. - Have features of both debt and equity.

Types:

Type Meaning Fully Convertible (FCD) Entire face value converted into equity Partly Convertible (PCD) Portion converted to equity; non-convertible portion remains debt, earns interest, repaid on redemption Optionally Convertible (OCD) Convertible at discretion of debenture holder

Conversion Details Specified at Issue:

  • Date of conversion
  • Conversion ratio (number of shares per debenture)
  • Conversion price (usually at discount to market price)
  • Proportion to be converted (for PCD)

Advantage to Issuer:

  • Lower coupon rate than pure debt (investor gets potential capital appreciation)
  • No repayment on maturity (shares issued instead)

Disadvantage to Issuer:

  • Dilution of existing equity shareholders' stake

Advantage to Investor:

  • Earn coupon income in initial stage (when project is nascent)
  • Benefit from share appreciation after conversion

docs.title: 2.2.7.3 Indian Depository Receipts (IDRs), Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) and American Depository Receipts (ADRs)
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Financial instruments that represent shares of a foreign company.
  • Traded in a market of a country where they are issued.
  • Denominated in local currency of that country.

Issuance Process:

  1. Company or investor delivers equity shares to a depository (foreign bank) in the target market.
  2. Depository places shares in custodian account in company's home country.
  3. Depository issues a certificate (Depositary Receipt) against those shares to overseas investors.

Sponsored vs Unsponsored:

Type Initiated by Listing Regulatory requirements Sponsored DR Issuing company Can be listed on exchanges Must comply with listing requirements Unsponsored DR Investor OTC markets only Less regulation

Two-way Fungibility:

  • Subject to regulatory provisions.
  • Shares bought in home country → converted to DRs in foreign market.
  • DRs bought in foreign market → converted to underlying shares in home country.

Country-specific DRs:

Type Market ADR USA IDR India HKDR Hong Kong GDR Multiple countries (typically EU)

Indian Context:

  • Indian companies can raise equity capital abroad via DRs.
  • Foreign companies can raise equity capital in India via IDRs (SEBI guidelines: lock-in, only resident Indian investors, etc.).

docs.title: 2.2.7.4 Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs)
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Foreign currency (usually USD) denominated convertible debt securities issued by companies in international markets.

Key Features:

  • Like convertibles, but generally optionally convertible.
  • Issued offshore in different denominations.
  • Regulated by RBI under FEMA (Issue of Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds and Ordinary Shares through Depository Receipt Mechanism, 1993).

Cash Flows:

  • Interest and principal repayment (if happens) → in foreign currency.
  • After conversion to equity → dividend paid in INR (currency risk lies with investor).

docs.title: 2.2.7.5 Equity Linked Debentures (ELDs)
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Floating rate debt instruments whose interest is based on returns of underlying equity asset (Nifty, Sensex, individual shares, or custom basket).

Structure:

  • Part of principal → invested in fixed income securities (principal protection)
  • Balance → used to buy options (exposure to equity returns)

Important Cautions:

  • "Capital protection" does NOT mean absence of credit risk (risk of default by issuer).
  • Credit rated by rating agencies.
  • If issuer uses proceeds for CAPEX, very little left after capital protection + options.
  • Better to engage an Investment Banker/Arranger to create this structured product.

docs.title: 2.2.7.6 Commodity Linked Debentures (CLDs)
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Floating rate debt instruments whose interest is based on returns of underlying commodity asset.
  • Most common: linked to precious metals (Gold, Silver).

Advantage to Investor:

  • Opportunity to earn return from commodity markets.
  • Initial capital protected.

docs.title: 2.2.7.7 Mortgage Backed Securities (MBS) and Asset Backed Securities (ABS)
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Debt instruments issued by institutions against receivables and cash flows from financial assets.

Examples:

Type Underlying Asset MBS Home loans ABS Auto loans, rent receivables, credit card receivables

Mechanism:

  • Cash flows from these assets → meet interest and principal repayment obligations on bonds issued.
  • Securitization creates liquidity from otherwise illiquid assets.

Features:

  • Credit rated.
  • May be listed on stock exchanges.

docs.title: 2.2.7.8 REITs/InvITs
docs.text:
Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs):

  • Pool money from investors.
  • Invest in revenue-generating real estate projects.
  • Formed as a trust.
  • Requirement: 80% of assets held in real estate assets.
  • Distribution: At least 90% of distributable surplus cash flow to unit holders.

Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs):

  • Pool money from investors.
  • Invest in revenue-generating infrastructure projects.
  • Formed as a trust.
  • Requirement: 90% of unit capital invested in revenue-generating infrastructure projects (directly or through SPV).
  • Distribution: At least 90% of distributable surplus cash flow to unit holders.

Common Features:

  • Enjoy favourable tax treatment if regulatory requirements met.
  • Issue units to investors to raise money.

docs.title: 2.2.8 Commodities
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Basic materials or goods that are largely homogenous in nature.
  • Interchangeable with other goods of the same type.

Example to distinguish:

  • Bar of gold = commodity (investor indifferent between bars of same quantity/quality)
  • Gold jewellery = NOT a commodity (buyer may prefer one design over another)

Types:

Type Meaning Examples Hard commodities Natural resources, mined or extracted Metals, crude oil Soft commodities Grown (agricultural) Grains, pulses

Investment Consideration:

  • Commodities and inflation are directly related → investing can help protect real value.
  • Most commodities involve huge storage cost → not suitable investments.
  • Certain avenues available to invest.

docs.title: 2.2.8.1 Precious metals
docs.text:
Examples: Gold, Silver

Why they are viable investments:

  • Help preserve real value of money.
  • Very long life (unlike many other commodities).
  • Storage cost very small compared to value.

docs.title: 2.2.8.2 Commodity ETFs
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Exchange Traded Fund that invests the pooled investment in a range of physical commodities.

How to invest:

  • Buy units of the fund.
  • Unit value moves with NAV of fund → moves with commodity prices.

Advantage:

  • Storage handled by the fund → investor has no storage obligation.

Most common:

  • Gold ETFs (easiest to store and manage).

docs.title: 2.2.8.3 Managed futures contract
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Portfolio of futures contracts that are actively managed by professionals.
  • Instead of buying actual underlying asset, investment managers take position in futures contracts.

How investor gains:

  • Buyer gains if price increases in future (and vice versa).
  • Can gain from price rise without buying the product.

Use:

  • Investors can invest in commodities through managed commodity futures contracts.

docs.title: 2.2.8.4 Warehouse receipts
docs.text:
Definition:

  • Document that shows proof of ownership of goods stored in a warehouse.

Key feature:

  • Most are negotiable → title to underlying goods can be transferred by simply transferring the receipt.
